headline: High risk of data leakage and cascading errors: ms-swift can read/write local files and call external APIs, while dbt-core can access warehouse data and emit outputs that may be reused downstream.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: A direct prompt-injection bridge is not documented. dbt-core has no clipboard/MCP/shared-channel surface, while ms-swift can read files and process stdin/stdout, so only manual or file-based bridging is plausible. The pair is therefore lower risk than shared-workspace cases, but uncertainty remains because ms-swift’s session isolation is not stated.
conditions: IF the operator manually copies dbt-core output into ms-swift prompts or files, injection becomes plausible.
IF both agents are pointed at the same untrusted text file, ms-swift may ingest attacker-controlled instructions.
mitigations: Keep the agents on separate workspaces.
Do not copy raw dbt output into ms-swift prompts.
Strip instructions from any shared text artifacts.
Use read-only exports for handoff files.
requires-engineering: add provenance tagging between tools.

B_data_leakage.rationale: dbt-core touches data warehouse data, and ms-swift handles datasets, logs, checkpoints, and secrets such as hub_token/sdk-token. Because ms-swift can read/write files and call external APIs, a shared workspace or copied artifacts could leak sensitive warehouse data or secrets. The exact default sharing is unstated, so this is medium rather than high.
conditions: IF dbt artifacts or warehouse extracts are placed in a directory ms-swift can read, leakage is possible.
IF ms-swift logs or uploads copied warehouse data to its API backends, sensitive data can leave the environment.
mitigations: Separate secrets and warehouse exports into different directories.
Disable or redact verbose logs before running ms-swift.
Use least-privilege tokens for any hub access.
Review files in the shared directory before execution.
requires-engineering: enforce workspace isolation and egress controls.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: dbt-core can call a data warehouse and ms-swift can execute shell commands, spawn subprocesses, install packages, and write files. Even though dbt-core itself has no filesystem write listed, ms-swift’s broad local mutation surface creates overlap on shared artifacts and configuration. Uncertainty about shared state and locking pushes this to medium.
conditions: IF both agents operate in the same working directory, they can overwrite each other’s configs or outputs.
IF dbt-generated artifacts are consumed while ms-swift is mutating the same files, race conditions can occur.
mitigations: Run each agent in its own directory.
Make shared inputs read-only.
Serialize access to any common artifact path.
Snapshot outputs before handing them off.
requires-engineering: add file locks or orchestrator-level coordination.

D_cascading_error.rationale: dbt-core can produce warehouse-derived outputs, and ms-swift can consume files/stdin and act through CLI or Python API. If dbt outputs are treated as authoritative inputs for ms-swift without verification, errors can cascade into downstream model training, evaluation, or reporting. The pairwise handoff is plausible but not directly documented, so medium fits.
conditions: IF ms-swift ingests dbt-generated tables, manifests, or logs without validation, upstream mistakes propagate.
IF ms-swift is used to automate reports or training from dbt outputs, incorrect data can cascade into actions.
mitigations: Validate dbt outputs before handoff.
Add schema checks on every exchanged file.
Require human review for derived metrics.
Keep raw warehouse extracts separate from model inputs.
requires-engineering: implement typed contracts between stages.

E_compliance.rationale: dbt-core touches data warehouse data, while ms-swift handles datasets, checkpoints, logs, and secrets and can call external APIs. If regulated warehouse data or EU PII is moved into ms-swift’s broader training/evaluation workspace, retention and residency controls may diverge. The profiles do not state certifications or residency, so uncertainty keeps this at medium.
conditions: IF regulated warehouse data is copied into ms-swift datasets, retention and access controls may mismatch.
IF EU PII is processed through ms-swift’s external API calls without a DPA, residency/compliance risk increases.
mitigations: Classify data before any handoff.
Block regulated data from ms-swift workspaces.
Use region-restricted endpoints where available.
Minimize retention of logs and checkpoints.
requires-engineering: document and enforce residency/retention controls.
